title: Sell more tickets than seats
allegory: Feature sparsity is like an airline overbooking a flight: because most ticket-holders rarely show up, two of them almost never turn up for the same seat, so selling more tickets than seats is a good bet.
map: a feature the model wants to represent
a dimension of the hidden space
how often a ticket-holder actually turns up
the feature probability p (sparsity is 1 − p)
two ticket-holders turning up for overlapping seats
two overlapping features active at once: interference
the chance of a clash, p × p
co-occurrence probability p², which shrinks much faster than the benefit p

chapters.name: More things than seats
chapters.note: five things to remember, two slots to keep them in

cap.1: There are far more things worth noticing than a layer has slots to hold them. Something has to give. What decides whether the model crams them in?
cap.2: A layer with d dimensions can hold d features cleanly, at right angles. With more features than dimensions it must drop some, or let them overlap.
cap.3: n features, d < n dimensions: orthogonal packing caps at d. The alternative is non-orthogonal directions that interfere, and the data's sparsity decides which the model picks.

cap.1: Airlines sell more tickets than seats because plenty of passengers never show. If people rarely turn up, clashes are rare, and overbooking pays.
cap.2: Features are sparse: each one is absent from most inputs. So a model can give more features than dimensions a direction, because overlapping features are rarely active together.
cap.3: Sparsity makes co-activation rare, so the expected cost of overlapping directions is small. That is the condition under which superposition beats simply dropping features.

cap.1: If each passenger turns up with chance p, two particular passengers clash with chance p × p. As p gets small, clashes vanish far faster than bookings do.
cap.2: A feature helps only when present (probability p); interference hurts only when two overlapping features co-occur (p² if independent). Cost per unit of benefit falls like p.
cap.3: For independent features of probability p, expected pairwise interference scales with p² while expected reconstruction benefit scales with p, so the trade tips towards superposition as p → 0.

marks.label: sparse: clash is a tenth of use

cap.1: Use falls in a straight line as passengers get rarer; clashes fall along a curve that hugs the floor. On the sparse side, clashes are almost free.
cap.2: At p = 0.1 a pair co-occurs 1% of the time, a tenth of the 10% each feature is on. At p = 1, dense data, every pair always collides, so overlapping never pays.
cap.3: p² ≪ p for small p. With dense data the model acts like PCA, keeping the most important features orthogonal; as p falls, extra features acquire directions.

cap.1: This is what sparse data looks like: most boxes empty, a feature or two switched on per example, and rarely two in the same row.
cap.2: generate_batch: for each feature in each example, flip a biased coin that lands with chance p. If it lands, give the feature a random magnitude; otherwise 0.
cap.3: Independent Bernoulli(p) masks times random magnitudes. Sweeping p across the n_inst dimension trains many models at different sparsities in a single loop.

chapters.name: Dense versus sparse
chapters.verdict: Same model, same loss. Only the data's sparsity changed the geometry.

cap.1: Same five features, same two slots. With busy data the model keeps the two most important and drops the rest. With sparse data it squeezes all five in.
cap.2: The sparsity sweep in [1.5.4]: dense data gives PCA-like behaviour; sparse data gives all five features directions, arranged as a pentagon. The change comes in sharp jumps.
cap.3: Superposition is a response to the data distribution, not an accident: vary only p and the learned geometry moves through discrete phases rather than sliding smoothly.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Sparsity is why neurons look messy
SAEs bet on sparsity to untangle them
Change the data, change the geometry

cap.1: Because real features are rare, models overlap them: one reason single neurons often react to several unrelated things. So we look for directions, not neurons.
cap.2: Sparse autoencoders exist because of this argument: if features are sparse, a wide dictionary with a sparsity penalty can pull the overlapping features apart again.
cap.3: Sparsity drives superposition and is also the lever SAEs use to undo it. Understanding it comes before reading, and then steering, features in real models.

coda.title: How rare do features need to be?

caption.1: Drag p down (rarer features) and watch the red clash curve collapse far faster than the green one. Then add features and see clashes climb.
caption.2: Clashing pairs grow with n² but shrink with p²; features in use grow with n and p. Sparse data, small p, is what lets many overlapping features coexist.
caption.3: E[active] = np, E[co-active pairs] = C(n,2)p², ratio (n−1)p/2. Superposition pays when this interference rate is small next to the benefit of representing extra features.

where_else: Superposition: the geometry a model builds when its features are sparse
Sparse autoencoders: dictionary learning that relies on features being rarely active
Compressed sensing and hash tables: fitting sparse things into fewer slots than there are things

hamming.what: The fact that most features are absent from most inputs, so any two of them are rarely active at the same time.
hamming.when: Whenever you ask why a model overlaps features instead of dropping them, or why an SAE's sparsity penalty can pull them apart.
hamming.why: Interference only costs when overlapping features co-occur, and co-occurrence shrinks like p², far faster than the benefit p of representing each feature.

object.title: The switchboard of rare lamps
object.subtitle: Rows are examples, pegs are features; a peg stands up only when its feature is on.

cap.1: Dense data: every feature is on in every example, so any two features sharing space collide every time.
cap.2: p = 1: all 8 features active in all 10 examples. Overlapping directions would interfere on every input, so the model keeps features orthogonal and drops the extras.
cap.3: Dense regime: every pair co-activates with probability 1, and the optimum is PCA-like.

cap.1: Half the pegs are up. Most rows still have several on at once, so clashes are everywhere.
cap.2: p = 0.5: each pair co-occurs a quarter of the time. Overlap is still expensive.
cap.3: p² = 0.25 per pair; with 28 pairs of 8 features, about 7 co-active pairs per example on average.

cap.1: Sparse data: most rows have one peg or none. Two pegs in the same row, a clash, is now the exception.
cap.2: p = 0.1: each pair co-occurs 1% of the time, about 0.28 clashes per example on average. Overlap becomes cheap.
cap.3: Expected co-active pairs C(8,2)p² ≈ 0.28 against 0.8 active features: interference is rare relative to use.

cap.1: From above: mostly empty rows. This is the world in which squeezing features together is worth it.
cap.2: This is the kind of data distribution that produces superposition in the [1.5.4] sweep.
cap.3: Superposition is a response to this distribution, not an accident of training.

predict.q: Features become ten times rarer (p goes from 0.1 to 0.01). How much rarer does a clash between a given pair become?
predict.why: A clash needs both at once, p × p. Ten times rarer each means a hundred times rarer together.

predict.q: Every feature is present in every example. What does the toy model do with 5 features and 2 dimensions?

options.t: Keeps the 2 most important and drops the rest

predict.why: With dense data every overlap costs on every example, so it behaves like PCA. The pentagon only appears once the data is sparse.

object.where: Anywhere capacity is shared by rarely simultaneous demands: airline seats, hash tables, shared bandwidth.
